question: A 39-year-old man comes to the physician with a 4-week history of lesions on his penis and scrotum. He has no pain or discharge from the lesions. Two years ago, he was diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia and was treated with imatinib. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and drinks one to two beers on the weekends. He is sexually active and had unprotected intercourse with a woman about 4 months ago while abroad on business. He appears well. His temperature is 37°C (98°F), pulse is 85/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Examination shows 3 nontender lesions up to 1 cm in size. A photograph of the lesions is shown. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
analysis: The patient presents with nontender lesions on the penis and scrotum, which have been present for 4 weeks. Given the history of unprotected intercourse and the characteristics of the lesions, the most likely diagnosis is granuloma inguinale, which is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. This organism is associated with painless genital lesions and is more common in certain geographic areas, aligning with the patient's recent travel history. Other options like Treponema pallidum (syphilis) typically present with different characteristics, and herpes simplex virus usually causes painful lesions. Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) would present with painful ulcers, and Chlamydia trachomatis typically does not cause such lesions. Therefore, the most likely causal organism is Klebsiella granulomatis.
